title: Causal tax policy response for Papua New Guinea is not identified

claims.text: No. The fiscal model is explicitly flagged with causal identification disabled, so its estimated agriculture-to-revenue relationship cannot be used to estimate a causal tax policy response for Papua New Guinea or any other country. The estimates are conditional scenario differences under a stated macroeconomic path, not causal effects of tax policy changes.

The fiscal model is a conditional government revenue transmission model trained on panel observations with features limited to sector growth contributions, lagged revenue growth, a trend, and a pandemic indicator. It contains no tax policy or fiscal instrument variables, so it cannot isolate how tax rates, exemptions, or administrative measures respond to or offset an El Niño shock.

The assessment frames its output as government revenue without the event minus government revenue with the event, conditional on the stated macroeconomic path. This is a scenario contrast, not a policy-response counterfactual: any endogenous tax policy action by authorities is not separately identified or modeled.

Convergence diagnostics pass for the fiscal model, but passing diagnostics support computational reliability only; they do not establish causal identification and must not be read as predictive skill for policy responses.

limitations: Causal identification is explicitly disabled in the assessment metadata for the fiscal model, so no causal tax policy response can be estimated for Papua New Guinea from this evidence.
The fiscal model includes no tax policy variables; revenue outcomes are modeled as conditional on sector growth contributions, lagged revenue growth, trend, and a pandemic indicator.
Historical validation is conditional on realized inputs and latest revised history; it does not demonstrate out-of-sample skill for policy interventions.
Price and exchange-rate responses are not modeled, and revenue includes grants, which further limits interpretation as a tax policy quantity.
The signed mean loss and the positive-part expected shortfall are distinct quantities; the shortfall applies only to the positive part of the loss distribution.
The evidence packet is fixed and bounded; no adaptive retrieval was available to obtain additional country-specific or scenario-parameter evidence.
